title: Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury: Respiratory Risk, Neurogenic Shock & Autonomic Dysreflexia
html:
Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) can rapidly threaten ventilation and spinal cord perfusion. The first nursing priorities are airway and breathing, control of possible bleeding, appropriate spinal motion restriction, repeated neurologic assessment, and early trauma or spine-specialist escalation. A person can have a spinal injury and hemorrhage or another cause of shock; do not explain hypotension as neurogenic shock until other urgent causes are assessed.

Learning goals

  • Recognize findings that suggest cervical or high-thoracic cord injury and impending respiratory failure.
  • Distinguish neurogenic shock (hemodynamic instability) from spinal shock (temporary neurologic loss of reflexes below the injury).
  • Explain why perfusion support, serial examination, imaging, and timely spine consultation matter.
  • Identify autonomic dysreflexia (AD) in a person with susceptible established SCI and act on a possible bladder or bowel trigger.
  • Plan prevention of pressure injury, venous thromboembolism, bladder and bowel complications, pain, and distress.

Initial assessment and spinal motion protection

After a high-energy fall, collision, penetrating trauma, or concerning low-energy fall, follow the trauma team's spinal motion-restriction protocol while protecting the airway. Avoid unnecessary movement and coordinate transfers with trained staff; do not delay lifesaving airway or hemorrhage care for a perfect immobilization maneuver. Record the mechanism, last known neurologic function, limb movement and sensation, level of any sensory change, pain, vital signs, and associated injuries. Repeat the same motor and sensory checks at defined intervals and after transfers or interventions. A new deficit, ascending sensory change, or declining hand strength needs immediate escalation. The specialist uses imaging and a standardized neurologic examination to define injury and stability; the nurse should not declare the spine clear based on a single normal observation.

Respiratory failure can develop before desaturation

High cervical injury may impair the diaphragm, while lower cervical or high thoracic injury may weaken intercostal and abdominal muscles. Observe respiratory rate, depth, work, voice strength, chest movement, cough, and secretion clearance. Paradoxical chest motion, weak cough, shallow breathing, inability to speak comfortably, or increasing fatigue is concerning even if oxygen saturation is initially normal. Escalate early for respiratory therapy and airway evaluation; prepare suction and ordered ventilatory support. Oxygen corrects low oxygen levels but does not replace ventilation or cough. During airway procedures, maintain spine precautions as directed by the airway and trauma teams.

Neurogenic shock is not spinal shock

Neurogenic shock is loss of sympathetic vascular tone after a high cord injury, often producing hypotension with relative bradycardia and warm skin. It is a circulatory problem that can impair cord perfusion. Spinal shock describes transient flaccidity and reduced or absent reflexes below an acute cord lesion; it is a neurologic phenomenon, not a synonym for low blood pressure. Both can coexist. In an injured patient, bleeding, tension pneumothorax, cardiac injury, and other causes of hypotension must still be sought urgently. Monitor perfusion, rhythm, urine output, temperature, and ordered laboratory or imaging findings. Give fluids and vasoactive medicines only under the resuscitation plan, avoiding reflexive large-volume fluid loading when neurogenic vasodilation is suspected.

The AO Spine–Praxis 2024 hemodynamic guideline suggests an acute SCI mean arterial pressure (MAP) augmentation range with a lower bound of 75–80 mmHg and an upper bound of 90–95 mmHg for 3–7 days; evidence quality is very low and recommendations are weak. This is a specialist-directed range, not an RN standing order or a reason to overlook bleeding, medication harms, arrhythmia, or individual contraindications. Record the ordered target and actual MAP trend, promptly report values outside the individualized plan, and reassess neurologic and end-organ perfusion. Early decompression within 24 hours is recommended as an option when medically feasible; the spine team determines candidacy and timing.

Autonomic dysreflexia: a different blood-pressure emergency

AD is most associated with established SCI at or above T6 and can occur after spinal shock resolves, although timing varies. A noxious stimulus below the lesion—most commonly bladder distension or a blocked catheter, or bowel impaction—may trigger abrupt hypertension relative to the person's baseline, pounding headache, flushing or sweating above the lesion, nasal congestion, and sometimes bradycardia. The person may have few symptoms, so measure blood pressure rather than waiting for a headache. Unlike neurogenic shock, AD causes hypertension, not hypotension.

If AD is suspected, call for help, check blood pressure and pulse frequently, sit the person upright and lower the legs if feasible and not contraindicated, and loosen tight garments or devices. Check the urinary drainage system for kinks, obstruction, or an overfull bag and correct simple problems within scope; follow the ordered catheter and bowel-management protocol and avoid maneuvers that add painful stimulation. If hypertension persists or is severe, the clinician directs short-acting medication and evaluation for other triggers. Continue monitoring after the trigger is addressed because blood pressure can recur or fall with treatment. In an unstable acute trauma patient, positioning and spinal precautions must be coordinated with the treating team rather than applied mechanically.

Ongoing nursing care and rehabilitation handoff

Track skin and device pressure points, use a repositioning plan that preserves spine precautions, and follow individualized venous-thromboembolism prevention orders. Assess bladder emptying and catheter function, bowel pattern, nutrition, pain, temperature regulation, and orthostatic symptoms during mobilization. Offer accessible communication, mental-health support, and early physical and occupational therapy consultation when stable. Never assume a lack of pain means there is no injury below the sensory level. Document the neurologic level and function in concrete terms so changes are visible across handoffs.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify injury mechanism, breathing effort and cough, limb strength and sensation, reflex pattern, blood pressure, heart rate, and potential bleeding or AD triggers.
  2. Analyze cues: Ask whether hypotension reflects hemorrhage, neurogenic vasodilation, or another cause; distinguish this from transient areflexia of spinal shock and later hypertensive AD.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Impending ventilatory failure, uncontrolled bleeding, cord hypoperfusion, and a new neurologic deficit outrank routine mobility or discharge tasks.
  4. Generate solutions: Coordinate airway readiness, safe spinal motion restriction, trauma and spine review, ordered perfusion support, serial examinations, and complication prevention.
  5. Take action: Escalate deterioration, perform ordered monitoring and treatment, protect the airway, investigate hypotension broadly, and remove an AD trigger within scope while seeking help.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm stable ventilation, adequate individualized perfusion, no new deficit, treatment tolerance, resolved AD symptoms and blood pressure, and a safe rehabilitation plan.

Clinical example

After a fall, a client has weak hand grip, shallow breathing, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, and heart rate 52/min. The RN keeps spinal precautions, calls the trauma and airway teams, assesses cough and ventilation, repeats a focused neurologic exam, and promptly reports the hypotension and bradycardia. Neurogenic shock is possible, but the team simultaneously evaluates bleeding and other trauma causes before choosing resuscitation. Months later, the same person with a high SCI develops a pounding headache and sudden hypertension with a kinked urinary catheter: that pattern suggests AD, requiring immediate blood-pressure monitoring, upright positioning when safe, and removal of the trigger within protocol.

Original educational synthesis. Immobilization, airway and hemodynamic management, MAP targets, surgery, catheter or bowel procedures, and AD medicines require current patient data, authorized orders, local protocols, and specialist supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, certification, or an official guideline product.
